sources.claim: FTC "Operation AI Comply" (September 25, 2024): five actions under existing consumer-protection law, including a company sold as a "robot lawyer" whose claims were alleged to be untested, a tool alleged to generate fake reviews, and schemes promising quick earnings from AI-powered online stores. On December 22, 2025 the FTC reopened and set aside the Rytr (review-tool) order; publishing fake reviews remains deceptive.

sections.skill: Spot exaggerated AI income, job or course promises

questions.prompt: Which is a warning sign in an AI offer?
questions.correct_answer: Guaranteed income
questions.intro: Some offers use AI hype to make big promises: "Earn 10,000 dollars a month with AI, no experience needed," "Our course guarantees an AI job," or "This AI lawyer replaces your attorney." Warning signs: GUARANTEED income or jobs, URGENT pressure ("only 3 spots left"), vague methods, testimonials you cannot verify, and upfront fees for "secret" systems. In September 2024, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced "Operation AI Comply," actions under existing consumer-protection law, including against claims about a "robot lawyer" and schemes promising quick earnings from AI-powered online stores.

sections.skill: Compare AI income claims with "get rich quick" ads in the past

questions.prompt: What did old "envelope stuffing" ads promise?

choices.text: A steady job with an established company, along with training, benefits and a contract

questions.correct_answer: Easy money with no skills
questions.intro: Long before AI, ads promised "Make thousands working from home stuffing envelopes!" The pattern was the same: easy money, no skills needed, pay a fee first to learn the "secret." Most buyers made nothing. AI income claims often follow the same pattern with new words: the tool is new, the trick is old. Recognizing the pattern helps you spot it whatever technology it mentions.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: Which search helps check a company?

choices.text: Its name plus "best ever," which will show the most accurate reviews from customers

questions.correct_answer: Its name plus "complaint" or "scam"
questions.intro: Checking a claim takes a few steps. Look for independent reviews, not just ones on the seller's site. Search the company name with "complaint" or "scam." Ask what exactly you get, what results past students actually had (with evidence), and the refund policy in writing. Compare with free or official resources. Remember that AI does not change basic rules: if an offer sounds too good to be true, it usually is.
